cards.explanation: Clinical benefit can include relief of symptoms even when a cure is unattainable.
cards.text: The clinical goal of gene therapy is to prevent or reduce disease by modifying genes or genetic {{c1::pathways}}.
cards.question: The clinical goal of gene therapy is to prevent or reduce disease by modifying genes or genetic {{c1::pathways}}.

cards.explanation: The sequence carries the therapeutic information. The delivery vehicle has a different role.
cards.text: An introduced DNA sequence intended to provide a clinical benefit is a therapeutic {{c1::transgene}}.
cards.question: An introduced DNA sequence intended to provide a clinical benefit is a therapeutic {{c1::transgene}}.

cards.explanation: Knowing whether one gene accounts for the phenotype helps define a realistic therapeutic goal.
cards.text: A disorder caused primarily by one gene is called {{c1::monogenic}}.
cards.question: A disorder caused primarily by one gene is called {{c1::monogenic}}.

cards.explanation: Changing one genetic factor may address only part of the disease process.
cards.text: If a disease involves several genes and environmental influences, it is {{c1::multifactorial}}.
cards.question: If a disease involves several genes and environmental influences, it is {{c1::multifactorial}}.

cards.explanation: A delayed effect can be inadequate even when a treatment has biological activity.
cards.text: In an acute illness, the time until a therapy begins to work must match the disease’s {{c1::time course}}.
cards.question: In an acute illness, the time until a therapy begins to work must match the disease’s {{c1::time course}}.

cards.explanation: The carrier and the therapeutic sequence have distinct roles.
cards.text: The carrier for therapeutic genetic material is called a {{c1::vector}}.
cards.question: The carrier for therapeutic genetic material is called a {{c1::vector}}.

cards.explanation: The term describes a route of transfer and says nothing by itself about clinical benefit.
cards.text: Transfer of genetic material into cells using a viral vector is termed {{c1::transduction}}.
cards.question: Transfer of genetic material into cells using a viral vector is termed {{c1::transduction}}.

cards.explanation: It is distinct from the clinical distinction between treating cells inside or outside a patient.
cards.text: Non-viral introduction of nucleic acid into a cell is commonly called {{c1::transfection}}.
cards.question: Non-viral introduction of nucleic acid into a cell is commonly called {{c1::transfection}}.

cards.explanation: Daughter cells may not all retain it, so the treatment effect can diminish.
cards.text: Genetic material present outside the chromosomes can become diluted when cells {{c1::divide}}.
cards.question: Genetic material present outside the chromosomes can become diluted when cells {{c1::divide}}.

cards.explanation: In vivo treatment takes place directly within the patient.
cards.text: When a patient’s cells are treated outside the body and then returned, the approach is {{c1::ex vivo}}.
cards.question: When a patient’s cells are treated outside the body and then returned, the approach is {{c1::ex vivo}}.

cards.explanation: Ex vivo treatment adds a stage in which cells are handled outside the body.
cards.text: Treatment administered directly inside the patient is described as {{c1::in vivo}}.
cards.question: Treatment administered directly inside the patient is described as {{c1::in vivo}}.

cards.explanation: The treatment is intended to benefit that individual.
cards.text: Gene therapy directed at a patient’s non-reproductive cells is {{c1::somatic}} therapy.
cards.question: Gene therapy directed at a patient’s non-reproductive cells is {{c1::somatic}} therapy.

cards.explanation: This distinguishes germline intervention from somatic therapy.
cards.text: Changing genetic material in gametes raises the possibility of {{c1::inheritance by future generations}}.
cards.question: Changing genetic material in gametes raises the possibility of {{c1::inheritance by future generations}}.

cards.explanation: Potential consequences extend beyond the treated individual.
cards.text: Heritable interventions raise a consent issue because {{c1::future generations}} cannot consent to the change.
cards.question: Heritable interventions raise a consent issue because {{c1::future generations}} cannot consent to the change.

cards.explanation: A lasting benefit therefore depends partly on the biology of the treated cells.
cards.text: Corrected cells can become more abundant when they gain a {{c1::selective advantage}}.
cards.question: Corrected cells can become more abundant when they gain a {{c1::selective advantage}}.

cards.explanation: The selective expansion discussed in the lecture requires a fitness difference.
cards.text: If corrected cells and uncorrected cells grow equally well, the corrected fraction need not {{c1::increase}} over time.
cards.question: If corrected cells and uncorrected cells grow equally well, the corrected fraction need not {{c1::increase}} over time.

cards.explanation: It is a potential source of harm in long-term follow-up.
cards.text: An unintended disruption at the site where therapeutic DNA integrates is called {{c1::insertional mutagenesis}}.
cards.question: An unintended disruption at the site where therapeutic DNA integrates is called {{c1::insertional mutagenesis}}.

cards.explanation: A response can affect both safety and sustained benefit.
cards.text: The ability of a therapy to provoke an immune response is its {{c1::immunogenicity}}.
cards.question: The ability of a therapy to provoke an immune response is its {{c1::immunogenicity}}.

cards.explanation: Duration of benefit and initial response are separate outcomes.
cards.text: A therapy that works initially but loses benefit during follow-up has limited {{c1::durability}}.
cards.question: A therapy that works initially but loses benefit during follow-up has limited {{c1::durability}}.

cards.explanation: Changing control of expression can have consequences without breaking the coding region.
cards.text: Insertional mutagenesis can affect a gene even when the insertion disrupts a {{c1::regulatory sequence}}.
cards.question: Insertional mutagenesis can affect a gene even when the insertion disrupts a {{c1::regulatory sequence}}.

cards.explanation: The concept had been proposed decades earlier.
cards.text: The first human gene-therapy trials discussed in the lecture took place in the {{c1::1990s}}.
cards.question: The first human gene-therapy trials discussed in the lecture took place in the {{c1::1990s}}.

cards.explanation: SCID includes several genetically distinct disorders.
cards.text: Adenosine deaminase deficiency can cause an autosomal recessive form of {{c1::severe combined immunodeficiency}}.
cards.question: Adenosine deaminase deficiency can cause an autosomal recessive form of {{c1::severe combined immunodeficiency}}.

cards.explanation: Severe impairment of adaptive immunity makes otherwise manageable infections dangerous.
cards.text: SCID stands for {{c1::severe combined immunodeficiency}}.
cards.question: SCID stands for {{c1::severe combined immunodeficiency}}.

cards.explanation: Other forms of SCID can have different modes of inheritance, including X-linked inheritance.
cards.text: The ADA-deficient form of SCID illustrates {{c1::autosomal recessive}} inheritance.
cards.question: The ADA-deficient form of SCID illustrates {{c1::autosomal recessive}} inheritance.

cards.explanation: His death in 1999 made safety assessment and informed consent central to the field.
cards.text: Jesse Gelsinger entered a gene-therapy trial for partial {{c1::ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency}}.
cards.question: Jesse Gelsinger entered a gene-therapy trial for partial {{c1::ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency}}.

cards.explanation: Partial OTC deficiency could be managed in this case, so research risks needed careful comparison with usual care.
cards.text: The availability of a manageable alternative treatment changes the {{c1::risk–benefit assessment}} for entering a trial.
cards.question: The availability of a manageable alternative treatment changes the {{c1::risk–benefit assessment}} for entering a trial.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from treating an illness or restoring lost function.
cards.text: Using genetic intervention to alter a non-disease trait raises the ethical question of {{c1::enhancement}}.
cards.question: Using genetic intervention to alter a non-disease trait raises the ethical question of {{c1::enhancement}}.

cards.explanation: Clinical effectiveness alone does not determine how a treatment should be distributed.
cards.text: Deciding who can obtain an expensive gene therapy raises a question of {{c1::equity of access}}.
cards.question: Deciding who can obtain an expensive gene therapy raises a question of {{c1::equity of access}}.

cards.explanation: Supplying a working copy and correcting the existing sequence are different outcomes.
cards.text: Conventional gene addition can restore a missing product while leaving the original disease allele {{c1::unchanged}}.
cards.question: Conventional gene addition can restore a missing product while leaving the original disease allele {{c1::unchanged}}.

cards.explanation: Gene addition can provide a functional copy while leaving the original variant in place.
cards.text: A treatment intended to change a specific DNA sequence in place uses {{c1::gene editing}}.
cards.question: A treatment intended to change a specific DNA sequence in place uses {{c1::gene editing}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture uses molecular scissors as an analogy for its role in editing.
cards.text: An enzyme that cuts a nucleic acid is a {{c1::nuclease}}.
cards.question: An enzyme that cuts a nucleic acid is a {{c1::nuclease}}.

cards.explanation: These technologies illustrate that targeted genome editing has several molecular forms.
cards.text: Zinc-finger nucleases and TALENs are examples of genome-editing platforms that predate {{c1::CRISPR–Cas9}}.
cards.question: Zinc-finger nucleases and TALENs are examples of genome-editing platforms that predate {{c1::CRISPR–Cas9}}.

cards.explanation: Compare the strands in the same chemical direction.
cards.text: A DNA sequence that reads the same 5′ to 3′ on both complementary strands is {{c1::palindromic}}.
cards.question: A DNA sequence that reads the same 5′ to 3′ on both complementary strands is {{c1::palindromic}}.

cards.explanation: They preserve information about previous encounters with foreign genetic material.
cards.text: Naturally occurring CRISPR systems participate in bacterial {{c1::adaptive immunity}}.
cards.question: Naturally occurring CRISPR systems participate in bacterial {{c1::adaptive immunity}}.

cards.explanation: The RNA contributes specificity while the protein provides nuclease activity.
cards.text: In the Cas9 system, sequence recognition depends in part on a {{c1::guide RNA}}.
cards.question: In the Cas9 system, sequence recognition depends in part on a {{c1::guide RNA}}.

cards.explanation: End joining instead reconnects DNA ends and can introduce small insertions or deletions.
cards.text: Repair that uses a matching DNA sequence as a template is called {{c1::homology-directed repair}}.
cards.question: Repair that uses a matching DNA sequence as a template is called {{c1::homology-directed repair}}.

cards.explanation: The repaired junction can contain small insertions or deletions.
cards.text: Repair that rejoins broken DNA ends without a homologous template is called {{c1::non-homologous end joining}}.
cards.question: Repair that rejoins broken DNA ends without a homologous template is called {{c1::non-homologous end joining}}.

cards.explanation: Its effect depends on its position and, in coding DNA, whether it changes the reading frame.
cards.text: A small insertion or deletion in DNA is often called an {{c1::indel}}.
cards.question: A small insertion or deletion in DNA is often called an {{c1::indel}}.

cards.explanation: It supplies a functional copy of SMN1.
cards.text: Zolgensma is a gene therapy for {{c1::spinal muscular atrophy}}.
cards.question: Zolgensma is a gene therapy for {{c1::spinal muscular atrophy}}.

cards.explanation: It is an example of a clinical application of gene therapy.
cards.text: Libmeldy treats {{c1::metachromatic leukodystrophy}}.
cards.question: Libmeldy treats {{c1::metachromatic leukodystrophy}}.

cards.explanation: It illustrates clinical gene addition for a defined molecular diagnosis.
cards.text: Luxturna is used for eligible patients with inherited retinal disease involving {{c1::RPE65}}.
cards.question: Luxturna is used for eligible patients with inherited retinal disease involving {{c1::RPE65}}.
